person.name: Emmy_Noether
person.summary: Emmy Noether (1882–1935) was a German mathematician whose work transformed abstract algebra and profoundly influenced mathematical physics. At Erlangen and later at Göttingen she developed the modern theory of rings, ideals, and modules, introduced the notion of Noetherian structures, and proved Noether’s theorems linking symmetries with conservation laws in physics. Barred for years from paid academic posts because she was a woman and Jewish, she nonetheless led a renowned school of algebraists before being dismissed by the Nazis and continuing her research and teaching at Bryn Mawr College and the Institute for Advanced Study in the United States.

events.title: Birth in Erlangen
events.description: Amalie Emmy Noether was born on 23 March 1882 in the Bavarian university town of Erlangen into a well‑to‑do Jewish family. Her father, Max Noether, was a prominent professor of mathematics, and her mother, Ida Amalia Kaufmann, came from a prosperous merchant family. Growing up in an academic household with three younger brothers, Emmy was surrounded from childhood by mathematical talk and university life, even as she was initially steered toward conventional domestic skills for girls of her class.

events.date_note: She passed the language teachers' examination in early 1900 and soon after chose to pursue university studies instead
events.title: Chooses mathematics over teaching
events.description: After showing talent in French and English, Noether passed the state examination qualifying her to teach languages at girls' schools, earning the top mark of "sehr gut". Instead of taking the secure teaching career this opened, she decided to study at the University of Erlangen, where her father taught, even though women were only allowed to audit lectures with each professor’s permission. This choice committed her to an unconventional and uncertain path in higher mathematics.

events.date_note: Bavarian restrictions on women's full matriculation were lifted in 1903; she formally re‑enrolled at Erlangen in October 1904
events.title: Fully matriculates in Erlangen
events.description: Following a year of study in Göttingen during the 1903–1904 winter semester, where she attended lectures by Karl Schwarzschild, Hermann Minkowski, Felix Klein, David Hilbert and others, Noether returned to Erlangen and formally enrolled as a regular student in October 1904. Now the only woman in her mathematics cohort, she committed herself wholly to mathematics under the influence of the invariant theorist Paul Gordan and began the research that would lead to her doctorate.

events.date_note: She completed and defended her dissertation in 1907 and received the degree summa cum laude later that year
events.title: Doctorate under Paul Gordan
events.description: In 1907 Noether received her Ph.D. from the University of Erlangen with a dissertation on [[invariant theory|invariant theory]] titled "Über die Bildung des Formensystems der ternären biquadratischen Form", supervised by Paul Gordan. The work, very much in the explicit computational style then dominant, contained hundreds of worked invariants and was awarded summa cum laude. Although she later dismissed this early work as "crap", the thesis established her as a research mathematician and provided her first publications.

invariant theory.explanation: A branch of abstract algebra that studies quantities or properties of mathematical objects that remain unchanged (invariant) under transformations from a given group, such as rotations or linear changes of coordinates.

events.title: Unpaid lecturer at Erlangen
events.description: From 1908 to 1915 Noether worked without pay at Erlangen’s Mathematical Institute, often substituting for her ailing father in lectures while pursuing her own research. She joined professional societies such as the [[Circolo Matematico di Palermo|Circolo Matematico di Palermo]] and the [[Deutsche Mathematiker‑Vereinigung|Deutsche Mathematiker‑Vereinigung]] and extended her thesis results to more variables, gradually moving from concrete invariant computations toward more abstract methods influenced by Ernst Fischer and David Hilbert. During this period she also informally supervised doctoral students, even though official credit still went to her father, reflecting prevailing barriers to women’s academic advancement.

Circolo Matematico di Palermo.explanation: An Italian mathematical society founded in 1884 in Palermo that became one of the most prestigious international centers for publishing mathematical research in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

Deutsche Mathematiker‑Vereinigung.explanation: The German Mathematical Society, founded in 1890, which served as the main professional association for mathematicians in German-speaking countries.

events.date_note: She left Erlangen for Göttingen in late April 1915 at the invitation of Hilbert and Klein
events.title: Moves to Göttingen amid opposition
events.description: In 1915 David Hilbert and Felix Klein invited Noether to Göttingen, then the leading center of mathematical research, to help them address algebraic problems arising in the new [[general theory of relativity|general theory of relativity]]. Her appointment was fiercely opposed by members of the philosophical faculty, who rejected the idea of a woman becoming [[Privatdozent|Privatdozent]], prompting Hilbert’s famous retort that a university was "not a bathhouse". Noether moved to Göttingen in late April, just before her mother’s sudden death, and began lecturing under Hilbert’s name, unpaid and without official status, while caring for her retired father during wartime.

general theory of relativity.explanation: Einstein’s 1915 geometric theory of gravitation, describing gravity as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy, replacing Newtonian gravity in most contexts.

Privatdozent.explanation: A German academic title for someone who has completed a habilitation and is authorized to lecture independently at a university, typically without a salaried professorship.

events.date_note: On this date Felix Klein presented her paper "Invariante Variationsprobleme" to the Göttingen Royal Society of Sciences
events.title: Establishes Noether's theorem
events.description: Soon after arriving in Göttingen, Noether solved a fundamental problem in the [[calculus of variations|calculus of variations]], proving what is now called Noether’s theorem: that every differentiable symmetry of a physical system’s action corresponds to a conservation law. Her paper "Invariante Variationsprobleme" was presented on 26 July 1918 to the Göttingen Royal Society of Sciences by Felix Klein, since she herself was not a member. This result became a cornerstone of modern theoretical physics, clarifying why quantities like energy and momentum are conserved and influencing later work in field theory and particle physics.

images.caption: First page of E. Noether's paper "Invariante Variationsprobleme" (Nachrichten von der Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen, Mathematisch-Physikalische Klasse 1918 (1918): 235-257. <http://eudml.org/doc/59024>), where she proved the homonymous theorem.

calculus of variations.explanation: A branch of mathematical analysis that studies how to find functions minimizing or maximizing quantities expressed as integrals, fundamental for formulating physical laws and deriving equations of motion.

events.date_note: Her oral examination took place in late May 1919, followed by the habilitation lecture in June
events.title: Habilitation and Privatdozent
events.description: After World War I and the 1918–1919 [[German Revolution of 1918–1919|German Revolution]] relaxed some restrictions on women, Göttingen finally permitted Noether to apply for [[habilitation|habilitation]]. She passed her oral examination in late May 1919 and delivered her habilitation lecture in June, thereby becoming a [[Privatdozent|Privatdozent]] in mathematics. That autumn she offered the first course officially listed under her own name, though she still received no salary, marking a formal but only partially recognized acceptance into the faculty.

German Revolution of 1918–1919.explanation: A civil conflict and political upheaval at the end of World War I that overthrew the German monarchy and led to the establishment of the Weimar Republic, bringing reforms including some expansion of rights for women.

habilitation.explanation: A post-doctoral qualification common in German-speaking countries that certifies the ability to teach and supervise research independently at the university level.

Privatdozent.explanation: An academic title in German-speaking universities for someone qualified to teach independently (usually after habilitation) who may offer courses but typically has no salaried professorial chair.

events.title: Founds Noetherian ring theory
events.description: In 1921 Noether published her landmark paper "[[Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen|Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen]]" (Theory of Ideals in Ring Domains), which recast the theory of commutative rings and ideals in a radically abstract form. She introduced and exploited the [[ascending chain condition|ascending chain condition]] on ideals, creating the class of "[[Noetherian ring|Noetherian]]" rings and modules that became central to modern algebra and algebraic geometry. This work inaugurated her second creative epoch, in which she systematized and unified disparate algebraic results into a powerful structural theory.

Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen.explanation: Title of Noether’s 1921 paper, usually translated as "Theory of Ideals in Ring Domains", regarded as the founding work of modern abstract ideal theory in commutative algebra.

ascending chain condition.explanation: A finiteness condition on a partially ordered set requiring that every increasing sequence of elements eventually stabilizes, which in ring theory restricts how ideals can grow.

Noetherian ring.explanation: A commutative ring in which every ascending chain of ideals stabilizes, equivalently every ideal is finitely generated; this class underpins much of modern algebraic geometry and commutative algebra.

events.title: Leads Göttingen algebra school
events.description: By the mid‑1920s Noether was the intellectual center of a flourishing algebraic school at [[Göttingen|Göttingen]], informally known through her devoted students as the "Noether Boys". In 1924 the young Dutch mathematician Bartel Leendert van der Waerden joined her circle, absorbing her ideas and later systematizing them in his influential textbook "Moderne Algebra", whose second volume was largely based on her lectures. Through her generosity in sharing problems and methods, Noether catalyzed major advances by students and colleagues in areas ranging from field theory to algebraic topology.

Göttingen.explanation: University town in Lower Saxony that became one of the world’s leading centers of mathematics and physics in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, attracting figures such as Hilbert, Klein, and Noether.

events.date_note: The International Congress of Mathematicians in Zürich took place in September 1932
events.title: Plenary address at Zürich ICM
events.description: In September 1932 Noether delivered a plenary lecture at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Zürich, a signal honor reflecting her status as one of the world’s leading algebraists. Her talk presented the latest developments in ideal theory and [[noncommutative algebra|noncommutative algebra]] to an international audience that included many of the foremost mathematicians of the day. By this time her reputation was firmly established, and figures such as Albert Einstein and Hermann Weyl publicly praised her as the most significant woman in the history of mathematics.

noncommutative algebra.explanation: A branch of algebra in which the multiplication of elements does not necessarily commute (that is, ab may not equal ba), with important applications in ring theory and quantum mechanics.

events.date_note: Following the Nazi seizure of power and the April 1933 civil service law, she was dismissed from her Göttingen post as a Jew and political suspect
events.title: Dismissed by Nazis from Göttingen
events.description: After the Nazi government came to power in 1933 and issued [[Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service|laws expelling Jews and political opponents from German universities]], Noether was summarily removed from her position at Göttingen. Her algebra seminar was abruptly dismantled, scattering her students and ending Göttingen’s dominance in algebra. Colleagues such as David Hilbert protested in vain, and the episode marked a devastating personal and professional break in her life’s work in Germany.

Law for the Restoration of the Professio.explanation: A Nazi law enacted on 7 April 1933 that ordered the dismissal of Jewish and politically unreliable civil servants, including university professors, from government employment.

events.title: Death in Pennsylvania
events.description: In April 1935 Noether underwent surgery in [[Pennsylvania|Pennsylvania]] for what was reported as a uterine or ovarian cyst and initially appeared to be recovering well. A sudden postoperative infection led to her death on 14 April at the age of 53. Colleagues in the United States and Europe, including Albert Einstein, wrote memorials emphasizing both the depth of her mathematical achievements and her unselfish, enthusiastic devotion to students and collaborators.

Pennsylvania.explanation: A U.S. state in the Mid-Atlantic region; at the time of this event, Noether was based at Bryn Mawr College in Pennsylvania, where she underwent the surgery and died.
